_format: Mount options the entry editor knows. n: name. fs: '@all' (every type except swap), '@local', '@network' or a list of types; not: types excluded from fs. cat: general, boot, desktop or filesystem. k: flag, value, or flag+value (value optional). v: value type: number, octal, size, text, choice, path, seconds; ch: choices; ex: example value; min/max for numbers. d: default (as shown to people). x: options in the same group exclude each other. a: set on the Access tab. alias: same as another option. warn: shown in yellow. t: mount sweep (tests/mounttest.cpp): skip (reason), with (extra options needed), value (value to test).

options.desc: Use the default options (rw, suid, dev, exec, auto, nouser, async). Written when no other option is set.
Read-only: files can be read but not changed.
Read-write (the default).
Writes are collected in memory and written to disk a little later (the default, fastest).
Every write goes to the disk immediately. Safer for drives that get unplugged without ejecting, but much slower and wears out flash drives.
Changes to folders (create, delete, rename) are written immediately; file contents still use the normal write cache.
Update a file's 'last accessed' time only when it is older than the last change, or once a day (the default; a good balance).
Never update a file's 'last accessed' time. Slightly faster and less wear on SSDs; few programs need access times.
Update the 'last accessed' time on every read. Only needed by a few old programs; causes many extra writes.
Use the kernel's default access-time behaviour (relatime unless set otherwise).
Turn relatime off (access times are then updated on every read).
Turn strictatime off and use the kernel's default.
Don't update access times of folders (already implied by noatime).
Update access times of folders (the default, following the atime setting).
Keep file time stamps in memory and write them to disk only occasionally. Fewer writes, same accuracy while the system runs.
Write time stamps normally (turns lazytime off).
Mount automatically while the computer starts (and with 'mount -a'). Set on the Access tab.
Don't mount while the computer starts; mount only when asked to (by clicking it, or 'mount <folder>'). Set on the Access tab.
If the device is missing or fails to mount, carry on starting the computer instead of stopping at an emergency prompt. Recommended for every drive that isn't needed to start the system.
The device needs the network (NFS, SMB, iSCSI): mount it only after the network is up, and unmount it before the network goes down. Network file systems imply it.
Allow running programs stored on this file system (the default).
Don't allow running programs directly from this file system. A good safety measure for data drives and shares.
Honour set-user-ID and set-group-ID bits (programs that run with their owner's rights). The default.
Ignore set-user-ID and set-group-ID bits, so a program on this drive can't gain extra rights. Recommended for removable drives and network shares.
Allow device files (special files that give access to hardware) on this file system. The default.
Ignore device files on this file system. Recommended for anything that isn't a system partition.
Any user may mount it, and only that user (or root) may unmount it. Also turns on noexec, nosuid and nodev unless exec, suid or dev come after it. Set on the Access tab.
Any user may mount it and any user may unmount it. Also turns on noexec, nosuid and nodev unless exec, suid or dev come after it. Set on the Access tab.
Only administrators may mount it (the default). Set on the Access tab.
Like 'user', but only the user who owns the device file (/dev/...) may mount it. Rarely useful on desktops, where udev owns the device files.
Members of the device file's group may mount it (e.g. the 'disk' group). Rarely useful on desktops.
Keep a change counter on every file, used by NFS servers and file integrity tools.
Don't keep a change counter on files.
Don't follow symbolic links while looking up paths on this file system (links can still be created and read).
Suppress some warnings from the file system driver.
Show warnings from the file system driver (the default).

Set the permissions of the mounted folder after mounting (e.g. 0755).

Mount only this sub-folder of the file system (path relative to its top).

Mount it the first time someone opens the folder, instead of while starting. The computer starts faster and doesn't wait for slow or missing devices. Set on the Access tab.
With automount: unmount again after the folder hasn't been used for this long (e.g. 60, 10min, 1h).
How long to wait for the device to appear while starting before giving up (e.g. 10s). Useful with nofail for drives that are sometimes unplugged.
How long the mount itself may take before it is cancelled (e.g. 30s).
Another systemd unit (or device path) that must be running first. If it fails, this mount fails too.
Mount this before the given systemd unit starts (ordering only).
Mount this after the given systemd unit has started (ordering only).
Start this mount together with the given systemd unit, instead of the usual file system target.
The given systemd unit requires this mount: it is started with it, and fails if the mount fails.
Mount whatever provides this folder first (e.g. the drive holding an image file).
Like requires-mounts-for, but this mount still goes ahead if that one fails.

options.desc: Create a swap signature on the device while starting if it has none.
Show this mount in file manager sidebars that follow the GVfs/UDisks convention, even outside /media.
Hide this mount from file manager sidebars that follow the GVfs/UDisks convention.
Name shown for this mount in file managers that follow the GVfs convention. Write spaces as %20.
Icon name for this mount in file managers that follow the GVfs convention.
Monochrome icon name for this mount (GVfs convention).
When this is mounted by clicking it in a file manager (UDisks), always ask for authentication, even for 'user' mounts.
Priority of this swap space: higher numbers are used first. Swap spaces with the same priority are used in turns.

Support access control lists (extra per-user and per-group permissions beyond owner/group/others).
Don't support access control lists.

options.warn: A power cut can corrupt the file system unless the drive has a battery-backed cache.
options.desc: Don't force ordered cache flushes. Slightly faster.
Write the journal (and so all pending data) to disk every this many seconds. Larger values mean fewer writes but more lost work after a power cut.

How file contents relate to the journal: 'ordered' writes data before its metadata (safe default), 'journal' journals data too (safest, slowest), 'writeback' doesn't order data (fastest; recently written files may contain old data after a crash). Can't be changed while mounted.
What to do when writing file data fails in ordered mode: log it ('ignore') or stop the journal ('abort').
What to do when the file system finds an error: switch to read-only, carry on, or stop the computer.
Tell the SSD immediately whenever blocks are freed. Usually better left off: Kubuntu trims all SSDs once a week (fstrim.timer).
Don't tell the SSD about freed blocks while running (the weekly trim still does).
Add checksums to the journal so a damaged journal is recognised during recovery.
Don't add checksums to the journal.
Write the journal's commit block without waiting for the rest. Only works together with data=writeback.
Choose where file data goes only when it is written to disk (less fragmentation, the default).
Choose where file data goes right away.
When a file is replaced by renaming or truncating, write the new data first, protecting against zero-length files after a crash.
Turn off that protection (slightly faster for programs that call fsync themselves).
Finish setting up a new file system's inode tables in the background; the number controls how gently (higher waits longer between steps).
Don't set up the inode tables in the background.
Longest time (microseconds) to wait for more writes to group into one journal commit.
Shortest time (microseconds) to wait for more writes to group into one journal commit.
Disk priority of journal writes, 0 (highest) to 7 (lowest).
Group (number) allowed to use the reserved space kept free for the administrator.
User (number) allowed to use the reserved space kept free for the administrator.
Use a backup copy of the superblock at this block number (for repairs; see 'mke2fs -n').
Turn on user disk quotas (same as usrquota).
Track and limit how much space each user may use.
Track and limit how much space each group may use.
Track and limit space per project (a folder tree).
Don't use quotas.
RAID stripe size in file system blocks, so writes line up with the RAID layout.
Don't cache shared extended attribute blocks (faster when many files have different attributes).
Check that metadata block numbers are valid before using them (protects against corrupted file systems).
Skip that check.
How many inode table blocks to read ahead (a power of two).
Allow parallel direct reads and writes without locking (the default).
Lock while doing direct reads (older behaviour).

options.warn: Unfinished changes in the journal are ignored; only use read-only, for rescuing data.

Same as norecovery.

Same as nogrpid.
Load the free-space maps in the background after mounting, so the first big writes are faster.

Access persistent memory (NVDIMM) directly, bypassing the page cache.
Mount this subvolume (path inside the file system, e.g. @home) instead of the default one.
Mount the subvolume with this number (5 is the top level). See 'btrfs subvolume list'.
Compress files as they are written, if they shrink: zstd (good balance, levels 1-15), lzo (fastest), zlib (levels 1-9). Already written files stay as they are.
Like compress, but try compressing every file, even ones that didn't shrink at first.
Defragment files that get small random writes (databases, browser profiles) in the background. Mostly useful on hard disks.
Don't defragment automatically (the default).
Tell the SSD about freed blocks: 'async' collects them and sends them in the background (the default on SSDs), 'sync' sends them right away.
Don't tell the SSD about freed blocks while running (the weekly trim still does).
